meta.title: Vietnamese Alphabet and Tones
meta.subtitle: 35 tones, letters and letter pairs · both directions, as two cards each
meta.desc: The first deck of the Vietnamese collection, and a short one. Vietnamese is written in the Latin alphabet, so there is no script to learn, but two things in it do not work as in English. The first is the TONES: every syllable carries one of six, marked on its vowel, and the tone changes the word — ma ghost, mà but, má mother (in the south), mả tomb, mã code, mạ rice seedlings. The second is a set of letters and letter pairs that do not sound as an English reader expects: the seven vowels with marks (ă â ê ô ơ ư, and đ), and d, gi, r, s, x, ch, tr, kh, g, ng, nh, ph, th, t, c and qu. The letters that sound roughly as in English (b, h, l, m, n) are left out. Each card asks both ways — the letter or tone, then its sound; the sound, then the letter — and gives one word that shows it, with its meaning and its pronunciation. The sounds described are those of the Hanoi standard, with the Saigon difference where the two part company: in the south, d, gi and v are said as y, r as an English r, s as sh, and the hỏi and ngã tones are one tone. Every word in the A1 deck names its tones beneath it, so this deck is the key to them. Sources: the sounds are the standard description of Vietnamese phonology; the example words' meanings and their IPA are English Wiktionary's, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0).

fields.Sound:
tone: ngang (no mark)
level, in the middle of the voice

tone: huyền (grave accent)
low and gently falling, often breathy

tone: sắc (acute accent)
high and rising

tone: hỏi (hook above)
falling from the middle of the voice, in careful speech rising again; in the south it dips and rises, the same as ngã

tone: ngã (tilde)
rising, broken by a catch in the throat, in the north; in the south the same as hỏi

tone: nặng (dot below)
low and heavy; in the north short, and cut off with a tightened throat
